source: AI Impacts: Evidence on good forecasting practices from the Good Judgment Project
finding: Skill persists across years: year-to-year performance correlation is .65 and about 70% of superforecasters kept the status next year.
numbers: Year-to-year correlation 0.65. About 70% of superforecasters retained status. Top 2% were labelled supers. Pay up to $250 per season, not tied to accuracy.
quote: the correlation between performance in one year and performance in the next year was 0.65
limits: Secondary summary by AI Impacts, not the primary data. 70% retention means about 30% lost status (regression and noise).
agent_relevance: Forecast skill is a stable trait, but not perfectly. An agent should treat past accuracy as a strong but noisy weight, not a fixed rank.

source: AI Impacts: Evidence on good forecasting practices from the Good Judgment Project
finding: Time horizon: superforecasters stay accurate further out than ordinary forecasters. Comparison-class reasoning had a measured payoff.
numbers: Supers at 300 days out beat regular forecasters at 100 days. Supers at 400 days about equal regulars at about 80 days. Comparison-class tag: Brier 0.17 vs 0.26 for the next-best tag (Chang 2016). GJP beat control by over 60% and beat an intelligence-community market by 25-30%. Structural model of dispositional, situational and behavioural variables: multiple correlation .64.
limits: Horizon figures come from a seminar talk quoted on the page, not a table. Tables 2 on the page were images and not read.
agent_relevance: Reference-class thinking is measurable. Long-horizon skill is rarer than short-horizon skill.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Design: five university teams competed in the IARPA two-year tournament. The Penn/Berkeley group tested training, teaming and tracking. All three helped; with statistical aggregation they won two years in a row.
numbers: Each year 2,200 to 3,900 forecasters (attrition 3-7%). Participants 83% male, mean age 36, 76% US citizens, 64% with some post-graduate study. 199 geopolitical outcomes over 2 years. Year 2: slightly over 200 per training x group-influence cell, 375 in the elite tracking condition (five super teams of 12).
limits: Volunteers with a bachelor degree and a 2-hour test battery. Not a general-population sample. Prediction-market arm not reported in this paper.
agent_relevance: The biggest levers were behavioural (training, team talk, selecting the best), not only maths on the output.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Probability training improved accuracy in Year 1 and Year 2. Probability training beat scenario training, which beat no training.
numbers: Year 1: F(2,1586)=14.29, p<.001. Probability vs scenario t(1053)=2.23, p=.026. Scenario vs none t(1056)=3.25, p<.001. Year 2: training F(1,882)=19.12, p<.001.
limits: Training was under one hour. Participants chose their own questions.
agent_relevance: A short instruction module on base rates, averaging and calibration is a cheap, replicable lever. The schema reference-class step has direct human evidence.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Teaming beat working alone. Team forecasters beat crowd-belief forecasters, who beat independent forecasters.
numbers: Year 1 group influence F(2,1586)=60.68, p<.001. Teams vs crowd-belief t(1036)=5.52. Crowd-belief vs independent t(1120)=5.92. Year 2 F(1,882)=62.76. More team comments went with better accuracy: r=-.19 (Year 1), r=-.22 (Year 2). Training x teaming interaction in Year 2 F(1,882)=5.78, p=.018; untrained independent forecasters were much worse than all other groups.
limits: Comment count is correlational (skilled teams may talk more). Teams attempted fewer questions than individuals.
agent_relevance: Structured exchange of reasons helps. For one model, teams must bring different evidence, not repeat samples of the same model (guardrail G4).

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Tracking top performers into elite teams gave the largest accuracy jump, with no regression to the mean in Year 2.
numbers: Table 1 last-week Brier (0 to 2 scale, lower is better), Year 2: supers 0.07, regular teams 0.16, individuals 0.24 to 0.26. First week: supers 0.25 vs teams 0.38 to 0.40. Supers answered 95 questions on average vs 61 for regular teams, t(270)=6.88.
limits: Supers also did more work. Selection is confounded with team support; Mellers 2015 tests this further.
agent_relevance: Select by past winning. For an agent, weight sub-processes by track record on resolved items.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Training and teaming improved calibration. All groups were overconfident, worst without training. The main calibration failure was unupdated 100% forecasts.
numbers: Calibration with training: Year 1 F(2,1586)=3.16, p=.04; Year 2 F(1,938)=3.78, p<.05; group influence Year 2 F(1,938)=7.07, p=.008. 100% forecasts made in the first 20% of a question life were right about 70% of the time; in the last 20%, about 90%. Year 1 forecast counts 29,997 / 27,477 / 25,844 (no / scenario / probability training).
limits: Overall calibration still described as remarkably good. Horizon dependent.
agent_relevance: Cap extreme probabilities early. Update as time passes.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Training and teaming effects hold across the life of a question.
numbers: Team forecasters Year 1 Brier by period (first week / middle 2 weeks / last week): 0.42 / 0.33 / 0.22 with no training, 0.35 / 0.30 / 0.19 with probability training. Individuals with no training: 0.44 / 0.40 / 0.31.
limits: Brier on the 0 to 2 scale, not comparable to the 0 to 1 scale used in LLM papers (halve it for binary).
agent_relevance: Normalise the Brier scale before comparing human and LLM scores.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: Superforecasters did not regress to the mean. Picked from the Year 1 top 2%, they were more accurate again in Years 2 and 3, while the next-best group and everyone else regressed.
numbers: Average of Years 2 and 3, standardised Brier: supers -0.34, top-team individuals -0.14, all others +0.04. Resolution .40 / .35 / .32. Calibration .01 / .03 / .04. AUC 96 vs 75 (all others). Comparison group of 1,498 other forecasters; at least 25 questions per tournament to be included.
quote: Defying expectations of regression toward the mean 2 years in a row, superforecasters maintained high accuracy
limits: Supers had more work and elite team support. Top-team individuals are not a pure no-team control. The label may itself motivate.
agent_relevance: Strong primary evidence behind the .65 persistence figure. Past score picks future score.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: The superforecaster edge holds under tough conditions (little time, little information) and they learn faster within a year.
numbers: First-day forecasts and forecasts made within 4 minutes of first seeing the question: supers still beat top-team individuals and all others. Learning slope in Table 1: supers -0.26 vs top-team individuals -0.18.
limits: Question difficulty controlled by standardising Brier within question.
agent_relevance: The advantage is not only more time. A fast first guess from a strong forecaster is already better.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: Superforecasters differ in fluid intelligence, knowledge and thinking style.
numbers: Supers at least 1 SD above the general population on Shipley-2 fluid intelligence. Higher than the other groups on Raven, CRT, numeracy, vocabulary, political knowledge, need for cognition and open-minded thinking. More likely to attribute close calls to coincidence than to fate.
limits: The Year 1 pool was already above average in fluid intelligence, so range restriction hides the full effect.
agent_relevance: Stable reasoning habits (check alternatives, accept chance) are part of the profile, not only knowledge.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: Superforecasters use finer probability steps, and coarsening their forecasts costs accuracy.
numbers: Unique probability numbers used: 57 for supers, 29 for top-team individuals, 30 for all others. Rounding to nearest 0.10 significantly worsened supers Brier; for the other two groups, accuracy fell only at rounding to 0.33.
limits: Correlational for the other groups; granularity could be a marker of skill, not a cause.
agent_relevance: Do not round forecasts to 10% steps when the evidence supports finer values.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: A debiasing training of under one hour (CHAMPS KNOW) improved Brier score 6 to 11% over control in each of four tournament years, with random assignment.
quote: Although the training lasted less than one hour, it consistently improved accuracy (Brier scores) by 6 to 11%
limits: Effect fell from 10-12% in Years 1-2 to 6-7% in Years 3-4. Volunteers. Year 4 means not copied because the PDF extraction was garbled.
agent_relevance: Randomised evidence for a prompt-sized intervention. Test the equivalent text in the agent.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Training worked partly through more forecasts per question (more updating). It did not work through more time spent.
numbers: Mediation by forecasts per question: significant in Year 3 (p=.001, n=213) but not in Year 4 (p=.20). Time on forecasting and writing: 4.1 h/week control vs 3.7 h trained, no significant difference. 6,622 control explanations vs 6,714 trained.
limits: Mediation analysis is correlational. It failed in Year 4.
agent_relevance: Gains come from process (updating, comparison classes), not effort.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Cognitive ability and practice made largely independent contributions. Training effects were not moderated by ability after Year 1.
numbers: Cognitive ability was the strongest individual predictor across all four years, and training was significant in all four. Only Year 1 showed an ability x training interaction (abler forecasters gained more); no significant interactions in Years 2-4. Self-reported comparison-class use linked to better accuracy.
limits: Ability was a composite of Raven, CRT and numeracy. Grit and open-mindedness added less.
agent_relevance: Training and ability add up. Training does not replace ability.

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov, Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Intelligence predicts accuracy before any track record exists. Correlations are small.
numbers: Season 1 (n=326): intelligence r about .20 to .22; CRT .20; actively open-minded thinking .13 to .17; political knowledge % correct .11; political-knowledge overconfidence -.15; education .13. Dominance weights: education 44.3%, intelligence 21.1%, cognitive style 18.6%.
limits: Several scales had low reliability (political knowledge .44, AOMT .64 in Season 1).
agent_relevance: For a cold start, use quick numeric reasoning tests as a weak prior only.

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov, Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Season 2 only partly replicated Season 1. Numeric intelligence replicated more strongly. Open-minded thinking and education did not.
numbers: Season 2 (n=547): Number Series r=.30, Berlin Numeracy .25 to .28, AOMT .00 to .04 (Season 1: .13 to .17), education -.03 to -.08 (largest Season 1 predictor), political knowledge .10, overconfidence -.14. Dominance: intelligence 56.4%, cognitive style 26.7%, age 13.2%. Joint model R-squared .11.
limits: Different sample and scales; AOMT Cronbach alpha was only .24 in Season 2, which may explain the null.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one trait. Only numeric ability replicated cleanly.

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov, Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Accuracy rankings are stable across question sets, and item-response models are about as stable as simple averages.
numbers: Season 1 (N=326): first 94 vs last 94 resolved questions, same metric across halves: simple .36, hierarchical .40, IRT .39 (within-half metric agreement .71 to .92). Season 2 (N=547): split at 199 questions, same design.
limits: Cross-half r about .4 is lower than the .65 year-to-year headline; different score (standardised ability on about 94 questions) and sample.
agent_relevance: Skill estimates need many resolved items. About 100 resolved questions gives stability of only about .4.

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov, Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Early on, traits help; with more resolved questions, past performance is the stronger predictor of future accuracy. Authors tested on out-of-sample data.
numbers: Authors report the shift in importance over time and validate on held-out data (202 forecasters, 64 questions in a Season 1 test set).
limits: Effect sizes in Brier points are small. Setting is a hybrid human-machine forecasting competition.
agent_relevance: Combine a cheap prior with updating on outcomes. A running skill estimate is the right shape.

source: Merkle et al. (2025) Identifying good forecasters via adaptive cognitive tests
finding: Short batteries of cognitive tests predict forecasting error at about r=-0.7 in a small sample and about r=-0.67 out of sample in a large one. Adaptive testing cuts test time.
numbers: Study 1: 170 participants from Facebook, 15 time-series questions each. Study 2: 1,194 participants, 36 questions, about 8 months later. Correlation of cognitive score with forecast error -0.71 (Study 1) and about -0.67 (Study 2, scored with Study 1 parameters; 0.99 agreement between scoring methods). Adding Shipley Abstraction and Raven gave -0.67. Denominator Neglect was the most informative test.
limits: Laypeople and time-series questions (not geopolitics). Correlation is higher than Himmelstein 2021 (about .2 to .3), perhaps because test and questions are closer in kind.
agent_relevance: Numeracy and denominator-neglect items are a cheap capability screen for any forecaster, including a model.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: A retrieval plus ensemble LLM system nearly matched the human crowd but did not beat it overall. Averaging with the crowd was best.
numbers: Test set Brier .179 vs crowd .149 (random .25); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Best baseline GPT-4-1106 .208. Earlier work (Zou 2022): 65.4% vs 92.8% crowd on a different set. System plus crowd average was best in every setting. RMS calibration error .42 vs crowd .38.
limits: Platforms: Metaculus, GJOpen, INFER, Polymarket, Manifold. Retrieval from news; test questions later in time than validation. Leakage concerns raised by Paleka 2025.
agent_relevance: Retrieval quality and ensembling are the levers. Defer to a crowd where it is confident.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: The system beats the crowd in a selective setting: when the crowd is unsure, early in a question life, and with at least 5 relevant articles. It hedges where the crowd is confident.
numbers: Crowd between .3 and .7 (51% of forecasts): .238 vs .240. Early retrieval dates: .185 vs .161. At least 5 articles: .175 vs .143. All three conditions (22% of forecasts, 43% of questions): .240 vs .247. Validation, crowd unsure: .199 vs .246.
limits: Rules chosen on validation data; wins are small and could be noise.
agent_relevance: LLMs under-use resolution. Know when to abstain.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
finding: An ensemble of 12 LLMs (median) matched the human crowd in a preregistered test. Models gain 17 to 28% from seeing the human median.
numbers: Study 1: 31 binary questions, 925 human forecasters, 3-month tournament. LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=.850. LLM crowd beat the 0.25 benchmark, t(30)=-2.35, p=.026. Mean model forecasts above 50% while outcomes were nearly even (acquiescence). Study 2: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 after seeing the human median (p=.003); Claude 2 also improved.
limits: Only 31 questions. The equivalence test at d=0.5 (0.081 Brier) was not preregistered. Humans were a lay tournament, not superforecasters.
agent_relevance: Aggregation helps LLMs too, but models from one family share bias. Watch for yes-bias.

source: Karger et al. (2024) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: On a leakage-free dynamic benchmark, superforecasters beat the public and every LLM tested. LLM score tracks general capability.
numbers: Overall Brier on the 200-question subset: supers 0.096 (39 supers, about 8 responses per question), public 0.121, best LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (p<0.001 vs supers). In another table: supers 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130; gap 0.054 vs 0.026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4. Chatbot Arena vs Brier r=-0.68 (p=.003), R-squared .47; parity near Arena score 1406 (CI 1346 to 1633). Compute fit r=-0.67 (p=.046), parity near 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28).
limits: Public survey about 49 responses per question; superforecaster sample small. Projections extrapolate a log-linear fit over few models.
agent_relevance: Target: beat about 0.096 on this set. Capability growth alone predicts a closing gap.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) LLMs are closing the gap on human superforecasters
finding: The superforecaster lead over LLMs shrinks by about 0.015 to 0.017 Brier a year; projected parity is late 2026 to 2027 but uncertain.
numbers: As of 29 Jan 2026, supers lead the best LLM by 0.017 difficulty-adjusted Brier (about one year of progress). Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) 0.117; Grok 4.20 preview (Oct 2025) 0.102. Parity extrapolated Nov 2026 (95% CI Jan 2026 to Nov 2027); dataset questions Jun 2026, market questions Aug 2026. A crowd-adjusted ensemble gained nearly 0.01 over its base. Supers sample and latest models share zero questions.
limits: Linear extrapolation that may break near the frontier. Human data last surveyed July 2024. A later Brier Index change moved parity to May 2027 (search snippet only, not verified).
agent_relevance: Test the scaffold against the current leaderboard, not old numbers.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters
finding: Claims of human-level LLM forecasting are fragile: temporal leakage and metric problems affect backtests.
numbers: Leakage routes: knowing the backtest date (questions kept because they resolved), search results that surface post-date pages, retrieval models trained on later data, model training data. Brier scores are not comparable across base rates; worked example: a base-rate forecaster scores about 0.125 on one mix while a clueless-on-rare-events forecaster who improves coin-flip questions from 0.25 to 0.15 scores about 0.1 and looks better. Accuracy is not a proper scoring rule.
limits: Position paper with examples. No new head-to-head human data. Halawi, Schoenegger and Phan are named as possibly too optimistic.
agent_relevance: Evaluate the scaffold only on unresolved questions. Report Brier, calibration and a base-rate-adjusted score.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Logical consistency of an LLM forecaster (negation, paraphrase, conditional checks) predicts its later Brier score without waiting for outcomes.
numbers: Consistency metrics correlate positively with ground-truth Brier on both benchmarks; some checks (conditional-probability consistency) reach R above 0.9, others give little signal. ArbitrageForecaster patches a base forecaster to enforce consistency. A companion benchmark resolves in 2028.
limits: Few models and question sets. Consistency is necessary, not sufficient.
agent_relevance: A code-checked instant proxy for skill that fits the scaffold: run consistency checks, no model judgement.

source: Forecasting Research Institute: Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) project page
finding: Superforecasters and domain experts did not converge on catastrophic-risk beliefs even after long structured debate.
numbers: 169 forecasters: 80 domain experts and 89 superforecasters. Disagreement largest for AI risk: experts gave much higher AI extinction risk; neither side moved much after months of debate.
limits: Project page only. Short-run accuracy numbers are in the working paper, not read. Long-run outcomes are unresolved.
agent_relevance: Short-run skill does not settle long-run priors. Do not treat supers as ground truth beyond the scored horizon.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert Political Judgment
finding: Founding result behind the GJP: experts did little better than simple baselines and foxes beat hedgehogs. Not read this session; cited as background by the GJP papers.
numbers: Not recorded (not opened).
limits: Not opened; do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Background for outside-view, many-small-ideas style.
